source_text:
{ΠΑΛΛ.} Ἴθι δὴ οὖν ὅποι φίλον· ὀνήσεις γὰρ καὶ μάλα πλουσίως.
{ΚΥΡ.} Συναγηγερμένων ποτὲ κατὰ τὴν ἔρημον ὑπὸ τὸ ὄρος τὸ Χωρὴβ, τῶν ἐξ Ἰσραὴλ, τὸν τῶν πρακτέων ἡμῖν ὁριστὴν διετύπου νόμον ὁ τῶν ὅλων Θεὸς, μυρία δὲ ὅσα καὶ ἐπωφελῆ θεσπίσματα προστεταχὼς, προσετίθει λοιπὸν, «Τρεῖς καιροὺς τοῦ ἐνιαυτοῦ ἑορτάσατέ μοι.» Τίνες δ' ἂν εἶεν τοιοίδε καιροὶ, διεσάφει πάλιν. Ἔφη γὰρ εὐθύς· «Τὴν ἑορτὴν τῶν ἀζύμων φυλάξασθε ποιεῖν· ἑπτὰ ἡμέρας ἔδεσθε ἄζυμα, καθάπερ ἐνετειλάμην σοι κατὰ τὸν καιρὸν τοῦ μηνὸς τῶν νέων· ἐν αὐτῷ γὰρ ἐξῆλθες ἐξ Αἰγύπτου· οὐκ ὀφθήσῃ ἐνώπιόν μου κενός· καὶ ἑορτὴν τοῦ θερισμοῦ πρωτογενημάτων ποιήσεις ἔργων σου, ὧν ἐὰν σπείρῃς ἐν τῷ ἀγρῷ σου, καὶ ἑορτὴν συντελείας ἐπ' ἐξόδῳ τοῦ ἐνιαυτοῦ, ἐν τῇ συναγωγῇ τῶν ἔργων σου, τῶν ἐκ τοῦ ἀγροῦ σου. Τρεῖς καιροὺς τοῦ ἐνιαυτοῦ ὀφθήσεται πᾶν ἀρσενικὸν ἐνώπιον Κυρίου τοῦ Θεοῦ σου.» Ὅτι μὲν οὖν τὸ χρῆναι πληροῦν τὰς ἑορτὰς τῷ Θεῷ, πρέποι ἂν ὅτι μάλιστα τοῖς ἀνδριζομένοις, καὶ οὐχὶ δὴ μᾶλλον τοῖς ἀναπεπτωκόσι καὶ ἄναλκιν ἔν γε δὴ σφίσιν ἔχουσι νοῦν, καὶ τεθρυμμένον ἀεὶ πρὸς τὰ σαρκός τε καὶ κόσμου, παρέδειξεν εἰπών· «Τρεῖς καιροὺς τοῦ ἐνιαυτοῦ ὀφθήσεται πᾶν ἀρσενικὸν ἐνώπιον Κυρίου τοῦ Θεοῦ σου.» Ἐποπτείας γὰρ ἄξιον τῆς ἄνωθεν καὶ παρὰ Θεοῦ τὸ ἀρσενικὸν, κατά γε τοὺς ἤδη προειρημένους τρόπους. Πλὴν ἐνομοθέτει χρησίμως τὸ χρῆναι πληροῦν ἑορτὰς ἁγίας. Ἔδει γὰρ, ἔδει τοῖς εἰς ἀρχὴν ἀναβαίνουσι παιδαγωγίας ὀρθῆς, καὶ ὑπὸ ζεύγλην ἤδη πως ἰοῦσι τὴν ὑπὸ Θεῷ, τῆς ἐν νόμῳ πολιτείας τὸ τέλος, ὅτι πάντη τε καὶ πάντως ἐκτελευτήσειεν ἂν αὐτοῖς εἰς τρυφάς τε καὶ εὐθυμίας, δῆλον δὲ ὅτι τὰς πνευματικὰς, εὖ μάλα παραδηλοῦν. Ταύτῃτοι προσηγορευκὼς τὸν νόμον, καὶ ἀποκρίνας ἀστείως τὸ πεφυκὸς ἀδικεῖν, ἐπαινέσας δὲ τὸ τελοῦν εἰς ὄνησιν, καὶ τῆς ἁνδανούσης αὐτῷ πολιτείας καὶ ζωῆς, παραθεὶς τὴν ὁδὸν, ὅτι καὶ καταλήξει ποτὲ πρὸς τρυφὰς ὁ πόνος αὐτοῖς, ἐφῆκε νοεῖν. Οὐκοῦν πρώτη μὲν ἑορτὴ κατὰ μῆνα τὸν νέον· δευτέρα δὲ ὥσπερ καὶ γείτων εὐθὺς ἡ τοῦ θερισμοῦ τῶν πρωτογενημάτων, τρίτη δὲ καὶ ἐπ' ἐσχάτοις ἡ ἐπ' ἐξόδῳ τοῦ ἐνιαυτοῦ, συγκεκομισμένων ἡμῖν τῶν καρπῶν, ἐν ἑβδόμῳ τοῦ ἔτους μηνί. Ἢ οὐχ ὧδε ἔφη τὸ Γράμμα τὸ ἱερόν;
{ΠΑΛΛ.} Σύμφημι.
{ΚΥΡ.} Οὐκοῦν ἀναγκαῖον, τὸ ἐφ' ἑκάστῳ καιρῷ παρακομίζειν εἰς μέσον, καὶ ὅπως τε καὶ ἐπὶ τίσι τελεῖσθαι πρέποι, διαθρεῖν ὡς ἔνι. Ἀπαίρειν μὲν γὰρ τῆς Αἰγυπτίων ἐκέλευε τότε τοὺς ἐξ Ἰσραὴλ ὁ φιλοικτίρμων Θεὸς, καὶ τῆς ἀφορήτου θητείας ἀποφορτίζεσθαι τὸν ζυγὸν, καὶ πρὸς τὴν τῆς ἐπαγγελίας μεθορμίσασθαι γῆν. Ἀντανίστατο δὲ τοῖς τεθεσπισμένοις ὁ Φαραὼ, καὶ ἀγροικὸν μὲν ἐφίει φωνὴν κατὰ τῆς ἀῤῥήτου δόξης, «Οὐκ οἶδα,» λέγων, «τὸν Κύριον.» Οὐκ ἀνήσειν δὲ τοὺς ἐξ Ἰσραὴλ διεβεβαιοῦτο πλειστάκις· καὶ δὴ καὶ πληγαῖς συχναῖς καὶ ἀλλεπαλλήλοις κατηκίζετο. Ἐπειδὴ δὲ ἦν ἀτεράμων ἔτι, καὶ ἄθραυστον
pass_a_gloss: PALL.: Go then wherever is dear (to you); for you will benefit (me) and very richly. CYR.: When once those from Israel had been gathered in the desert under the mountain Horeb, the God of all was shaping the law that defines for us the things to be done, and having commanded countless and beneficial decrees, he added next: 'three seasons of the year feast for me.' And what such seasons would be he made clear again. For he said at once: 'the feast of the unleavened take care to do; seven days you will eat unleavened (bread), just as I commanded you according to the season of the month of the new (things); for in it you went out from Egypt; you will not be seen before me empty; and a feast of the harvest of firstfruits you will do of your works, which you sow in your field, and a feast of completion at the exit of the year, in the gathering of your works from your field. Three seasons of the year every male will be seen before the Lord your God.' That the having to fulfill the feasts to God would befit most those acting manfully, and surely not rather those who have fallen back and have an unwarlike mind in themselves, and always enervated toward the things of the flesh and world, he showed by saying 'three seasons of the year every male will be seen before the Lord your God.' For the male is worthy of the oversight from above and from God, according to the manners already said before. Except that he legislated usefully the having to fulfill holy feasts. For it was needful, needful, to show very well to those going up to the beginning of right pedagogy, and already somehow going under the yoke under God, the end of the conduct in law, that wholly and altogether it would end for them in delights and good cheer, and clearly the spiritual ones. On this account, having addressed the law, and having neatly separated what is naturally disposed to do wrong, and having praised what accomplishes toward benefit, and having set beside the way of the conduct and life pleasing to him, he allowed (them) to understand that the toil also will end at some time in delights for them. Therefore first feast in the new month; second, as also a neighbor at once, the (feast) of the harvest of the firstfruits, third and at the last the one at the exit of the year, the fruits having been gathered for us, in the seventh month of the year. Or did the sacred Letter not say thus? PALL.: I agree. CYR.: Therefore (it is) necessary to bring into the middle the thing at each season, and to examine as is possible both how and on what (grounds) it would befit to be fulfilled. For the pitying God then commanded those from Israel to depart from the (land) of the Egyptians and to unload the yoke of the unbearable servitude and to move across toward the land of the promise. But Pharaoh stood against the decrees and let loose a boorish voice against the ineffable glory, saying 'I do not know the Lord.' And he affirmed many times that he would not let go those from Israel; and indeed he was also maltreated by frequent and successive blows. And since he was still unsoftened, and unbroken (madness he practiced...) (continues).
pass_b_english: Palladius: Go on, then, wherever you please; you will do me good, and very richly.

Cyril: Once, when those of Israel had been gathered in the wilderness below Mount Horeb, the God of all laid down for us the law that marks out what we must do. And after he had commanded countless decrees, and profitable ones, he then added: ‘Three times a year keep a feast to me’ (Exodus 23:14). What these times were he made clear in turn, for he said at once: ‘Take care to keep the feast of unleavened bread. Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you, at the season of the month of new grain; for in it you came out of Egypt. You shall not appear before me empty. And you shall keep the feast of the harvest of the firstfruits of your labors, of whatever you sow in your field, and the feast of completion at the end of the year, when you gather in your labors from your field. Three times a year every male of yours shall appear before the Lord your God’ (Exodus 23:15–17).

That keeping the feasts for God would be most fitting for those who play the man, and not rather for those who are slack and have a feeble mind in them, always softened toward the things of the flesh and of the world, he showed by saying: ‘Three times a year every male of yours shall appear before the Lord your God.’ For what is male is worthy of oversight from above and from God, in the ways already described. Yet he legislated usefully that holy feasts must be kept. For it was needful, truly needful, to show very plainly to those who were climbing to the beginning of a right training, and were already somehow coming under the yoke of God, the end of the life under the law: that in every way and at all events it would end for them in delights and gladness, plainly spiritual ones. That is why, after he had proclaimed the law, had neatly set apart what by its nature does wrong, had praised what leads to profit, and had set before them the way of the conduct and life that pleases him, he let them understand that their labor would one day end in delights. So the first feast is in the month of new grain; the second, a close neighbor, comes at once, the feast of the harvest of the firstfruits; and the third and last is the feast at the end of the year, when our fruits have been gathered in, in the seventh month of the year. Or is that not what the sacred Writing said?

Cyril: Then we must bring forward what belongs to each season, and examine, as far as we can, how and on what grounds it is fitting for it to be kept. At that time the compassionate God was commanding those of Israel to depart from the land of the Egyptians, to throw off the yoke of an unbearable servitude, and to move across to the land of promise. But Pharaoh set himself against what had been decreed. He let loose a boorish word against the ineffable glory, saying, ‘I do not know the Lord’ (Exodus 5:2), and he declared again and again that he would not let those of Israel go; and so he was punished with plague upon plague, one after another. choices.term: κατὰ τὸν καιρὸν τοῦ μηνὸς τῶν νέων
choices.english: at the season of the month of new grain
choices.why: LXX name for Abib; Cyril reuses 'the new month' for the first feast.

choices.term: ἄθραυστον | ἐμελέτα κατὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ τὴν ἀπόνοιαν
choices.english: and his unbroken… (continued in §3: madness he kept up against God)
choices.why: The column break falls between adjective and noun; the English stops at the same place.
Cyril reads 'male' morally (manly vigor), as in earlier books.
